evaluation.positioning_hook: A London neurosurgeon who develops a craving for human brains must hide her condition, protect her brother, and outmaneuver a homicide detective while hunting predators who deserve to die.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is instantly legible and built for genre buyers: a surgeon-turned-brain-craver with a vigilante edge, set against London crime and elite hypocrisy. The audience is narrower than a broad procedural because the cannibal premise is extreme, but the premise is sticky and easy to pitch.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The pilot lands its engine early: Sylvie wakes changed, tests the condition, and realizes she can only function after feeding. The final beat with Harry and the detective pressure confirms the series question cleanly.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sylvie is a strong lead: high-achieving, morally rigid, physically compromised, and increasingly dangerous to herself and others. Jett, Akin, Medea, and Harry all have enough friction to keep the engine alive around her.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a rare tonal mash-up: medical precision, gothic London, social satire, and body-horror appetite. The brain-eating condition is not just a gimmick; it is tied to class, justice, and female fear in a way that feels authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The pilot moves with real escalation from grave-robbing to diagnosis to murder to the final Harry reveal. It does spend time on banter and atmosphere, but the case-of-the-week pressure and the condition reveal keep the momentum intact.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The show’s core contradiction is memorable and immediately ownable: a surgeon who becomes a predator in order to keep doing good. The idea lands fast and keeps generating new story turns, especially once the detective and the sex-trafficker target enter the same orbit.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: London here is not generic backdrop; it has class markers, institutional pressure, nightlife, parks, hospitals, and elite enclaves that all feed story. The hospital, Met, and activist/consumer spaces create a layered world with recurring friction.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is sharply specific: gothic, filthy-funny, and socially observant, with a strong British register. The script can pivot from surgical detail to cannibal farce to genuine dread without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The pilot hints at more than the monster premise: Sylvie’s scars, Medea’s mentorship, Harry’s trouble, and the institutional corruption around Simeon Black all suggest deeper season-long payoffs. The mythology is still mostly implied rather than fully articulated, which keeps this in the solid rather than exceptional range.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Sylvie/Jett is a durable engine, and Akin/Medea/Harry add meaningful pressure points rather than just function. It is still lead-centered, but the supporting cast has enough personality and conflict to generate repeatable scenes.

lead_characters.name: Sylvie Bardo
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 20s; London-based neurosurgeon from a South London estate; working-class, vegan-turned-cannibal, white British.
lead_characters.hook: A brilliant, tightly wound neurosurgeon who lives by discipline until a bite in Victoria Park turns her into someone who craves human brains. She is morally serious, class-mobile, and deeply protective of patients and family, which makes her condition both a private horror and a public threat. Her clipped, surgical competence is constantly at war with the animal urgency underneath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve — a role that lets an actor play intelligence, volatility, physical comedy, and moral fracture in the same hour. It also gives the kind of transformation role that can reset how the industry sees a performer: prestige lead, genre engine, and antihero all at once.

lead_characters.name: Jett Devi
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 20s; Londoner of South Asian heritage; stylish, queer-coded, entrepreneurial, working-class.
lead_characters.hook: Sylvie’s ride-or-die best friend and the show’s chaos engine: filthy funny, sexually fluent, and far more practical than she first appears. She runs on loyalty, hustle, and gallows humor, with an OnlyFans side hustle and a real instinct for survival. She is the one person who can keep Sylvie grounded while also helping her cross lines.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing best-friend role that Ayo Edebiri in The Bear or Michaela Coel in Chewing Gum made feel electric — fast, funny, emotionally legible, and never just comic relief. It gives an actor the chance to own the room, land the jokes, and reveal real loyalty under the swagger.

lead_characters.name: Akin Okoye
lead_characters.demographics: Man, mid-30s; Black British detective, uniformed then moving into homicide; professional, controlled, under political pressure.
lead_characters.hook: A homicide detective with a conscience and a bruised career, forced to clean up after institutional failure while trying to read Sylvie before she reads him. He is observant, dry, and increasingly intrigued by the surgeon who keeps turning up at the center of violent events. The role carries authority without making him invulnerable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the grounded, quietly magnetic authority of Idris Elba in Luther — a detective role that plays intelligence, restraint, and moral fatigue rather than just procedure. It gives an actor the chance to carry suspicion, wit, and romantic tension without ever losing the job.

lead_characters.name: Medea Green
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 50s; senior surgeon and mentor; white British; institutionally powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Sylvie’s mentor and gatekeeper, a woman who climbed the ladder and knows exactly how the hospital works. She is sharp, politically savvy, and not sentimental about ambition, but she still sees Sylvie’s talent and vulnerability. She embodies the cost of surviving the system from inside it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of formidable mentor role that Olivia Colman in The Crown or Harriet Walter in Succession turns into a masterclass in authority and subtext. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing power, history, and private calculation in every exchange.

lead_characters.name: Harry Bardo
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late teens; Sylvie’s younger brother; London working-class, trouble-prone.
lead_characters.hook: Sylvie’s younger brother, a charming liability whose off-screen trouble keeps pulling her back into family duty. He is not just a plot complication; he is the emotional tether to the life Sylvie is trying to outrun. The final reveal with the gun makes him a real pressure point, not a decorative sibling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of volatile younger-brother role that Jack O’Connell in Skins or Barry Keoghan in The Banshees of Inisherin made memorable — messy, dangerous, and unexpectedly vulnerable. It gives an actor a chance to be both a problem and a heartbreak.

lead_characters.name: Guy Lively
lead_characters.demographics: Man, early 30s; surgeon; privileged, polished, socially fluent.
lead_characters.hook: Sylvie’s colleague and fiancé, a polished hospital insider who looks like a safe choice until the script starts revealing how much he benefits from not seeing what’s in front of him. He is charming, entitled, and useful as a mirror for Sylvie’s self-denial. The role is less villain than pressure valve for her double life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of polished-but-dodgy romantic role that Tom Hiddleston in The Night Manager or Matthew Goode in A Discovery of Witches can make feel seductive and suspect at once. It gives an actor the chance to play charm as a weapon and insecurity as a tell.

lead_characters.name: Niamh Larkin
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 20s; detective sergeant; Irish, cheerful, sharp, unbothered by gore.
lead_characters.hook: Akin’s junior partner, all appetite and banter, who brings levity without losing competence. She is socially disarming, observant, and already clocking more than she says. She helps make the police world feel lived-in rather than procedural wallpaper.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakout sidekick role that Daisy Edgar-Jones in Normal People or Aisling Bea in This Way Up showed can become a fan favorite fast — warm, funny, and quietly sharp. It gives an actor a chance to steal scenes while still serving the case.

lead_characters.name: Medea
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 50s; senior surgeon and mentor; white British; institutionally powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Sylvie’s mentor and gatekeeper, a woman who climbed the ladder and knows exactly how the hospital works. She is sharp, politically savvy, and not sentimental about ambition, but she still sees Sylvie’s talent and vulnerability. She embodies the cost of surviving the system from inside it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of formidable mentor role that Olivia Colman in The Crown or Harriet Walter in Succession turns into a masterclass in authority and subtext. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing power, history, and private calculation in every exchange.

lead_characters.name: Coriolanus Spark
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 60s; pathologist; older British male, eccentric professional.
lead_characters.hook: The hospital’s pathologist, a wry, observant elder who notices what others miss and says it sideways. He functions as a quiet truth-teller in a world of euphemism and institutional spin. He also gives the series a useful older male counterpoint to the younger leads.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of dry, scene-rich supporting role that Jim Broadbent in Iris or David Bradley in Broadchurch can turn into instant texture. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing wit, authority, and unease in a few well-placed scenes.

lead_characters.name: Apple
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 20s; server; working-class, young, observant.
lead_characters.hook: A server at Carnivoyeur who clocks the room fast and has just enough attitude to survive it. She is a small but vivid witness to the show’s class and gender dynamics, and she gives Sylvie a human point of contact inside the restaurant world. The role is brief but memorable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the kind of sharp, compact scene-stealing energy that let Anya Taylor-Joy in The Menu or Jodie Comer in early Killing Eve turn a few moments into a calling card. It gives an actor a clean, high-impact showcase in a single sequence.

lead_characters.name: Candy
lead_characters.hook: Jett’s salon contact and a small but vivid piece of the show’s London texture. She is brisk, unsentimental, and not impressed by anyone’s drama, which makes her a useful reality check in a heightened series. She helps ground the world in ordinary labor and attitude.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of lived-in supporting role that Lesley Manville or Sharon D. Clarke can make unforgettable with very little screen time. It gives an actor a chance to build a whole person out of attitude, rhythm, and one or two killer exchanges.

casting_characteristics: late-20s female lead with strong comedic and physical range
supporting detective and hospital ensemble with age-specific authority roles
no child performer requirement in the pilot

notable_requirements: gym, spa, restaurant, and flat interiors

technical.vfx_details: Primarily practical gore and blood effects with limited enhancement for the brain-eating, wound, and corpse imagery.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood, gore, prosthetic wound work, corpse makeup, and practical animal handling for dog/badger beats.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Serialized; each episode can braid Sylvie's condition, a homicide investigation, and institutional corruption with a recurring predator-of-the-week pressure.

budget.note: Contemporary London is manageable, but the pilot leans on multiple night exteriors, a cemetery grave-digging sequence, practical gore, a townhouse break-in, and dog/badger beats that need careful scheduling.

casting.note: The lead needs to play surgical authority, physical comedy, erotic discomfort, and predatory menace in one role; Jett and Akin also need actors with strong comic timing and authority.

development.note: The pilot’s engine is clear, but the series is balancing medical thriller, cannibal horror, and corruption drama in the same hour, which makes tone management a real buyer conversation.

comp_set.why_it_comps: A professional woman whose appetite becomes the engine for solving violent cases, with genre playfulness layered over procedural structure.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated genre with a female antihero, dark humor, and a strong London crime backdrop.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, slightly female, urban, streamer-native, with appetite for prestige horror and crime hybrids.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary London locations, a hospital ensemble, practical gore, and significant night work keep this in mid-tier series territory.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building female-led genre
premium cable drama buyers with horror tolerance
boutique genre producers with prestige aspirations
buyers seeking darkly comic antihero series
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character-first genre can still be sold on premise. The hospital setting, London specificity, and cannibal-vigilante contradiction make it feel premium rather than disposable.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone series rather than a franchise engine; no clear spinoff character or alternate-world vector is established on the page.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand and pitch the show in one sentence, which is a real advantage in a crowded genre market. That clarity helps attract streamer dev execs and actors who want a role with a sharp hook.
strengths.evidence: Sylvie’s first-person medical competence collides with a literal craving for human brains, and the pilot immediately tests that condition in the graveyard, the hospital, and the restaurant.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sylvie is a premium lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part offers range: authority, repression, physical deterioration, black comedy, and moral collapse. That is the kind of role that can pull a name actor or launch a breakout.
strengths.evidence: She moves from precise neurosurgical language to drooling mid-operation, then to predatory feeding and finally to a terrified attempt to contain herself.

strengths.what_it_means: The show has a real sense of place, class, and institutional hierarchy, which makes the world feel bigger than the pilot. That gives buyers confidence the series can keep finding new pressure points without leaving its lane.
strengths.evidence: Highgate Cemetery, St Gertrude’s, New Scotland Yard, Victoria Park, Kensington, and the restaurant world all carry distinct social texture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Sylvie-Jett friendship is a durable engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The series has a built-in two-hander dynamic that can generate banter, cover-ups, and emotional stakes beyond the central monster premise. That makes the show easier to sustain and easier to cast around.
strengths.evidence: Jett helps Sylvie test diets, hide evidence, plan the Simeon Black hit, and absorb the moral fallout while still sounding like a real best friend.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The detective thread adds procedural traction.
strengths.what_it_means: Akin gives the show a clean law-enforcement spine without turning it into a standard case-of-the-week. That broadens the buyer conversation to include crime buyers who want a genre edge.
strengths.evidence: Akin links the grave, the park killing, and Sylvie’s hospital presence into a single investigation while already suspecting something is off.

whats_special.headline: This is a premium-streaming, female-led horror-crime series with a killer one-line hook, a breakout lead role, and a London-specific world that feels expensive in texture rather than scale. The pilot’s combination of contained locations, practical gore, and a strong friendship engine makes it especially attractive to buyers who want elevated genre without tentpole spend.

items.area: The cannibal premise narrows the buyer pool.
items.detail: The show is commercially legible, but the human-brain appetite is still a hard sell outside streamer and premium-cable lanes. That makes the premise a strong hook and a real filter at the same time.

items.area: The pilot leans on a lot of tonal switching.
items.detail: The script moves from gothic grave-robbing to medical realism to broad banter to body-horror feeding to police procedural. That range is part of the appeal, but it also means buyers will immediately ask how the series keeps its center of gravity.

OnlyFans, Hyrox, Sweaty Betty, Agent Provocateur, Marlborough Pinot Noir, Black Bowmore, Jo Malone, Lynx Africa, and K-Pop all appear in dialogue or scene texture. None of them are deal-breakers on their own, but they create a real business affairs pass before greenlight.

items.area: Sylvie carries the whole show’s credibility.
items.detail: The pilot asks one actor to play surgical authority, physical decline, romantic tension, black comedy, and predatory menace in the same hour. That is a major upside if cast right, but it is also the single biggest casting conversation on the project.

issues.headline: The project’s main friction is not clarity; it is buyer appetite. The premise is memorable, but the cannibal engine, brand-clearance clutter, and tonal range will make every greenlight conversation about whether the package can land the right lead and the right platform.
